notes.meaning: These verses name families of the temple servants, also known as the Nethinim. Their ancestors were given to help the Levites with daily practical chores at the house of God. Even though their work was humble, God recorded each family by name and brought them safely back to Jerusalem.

The list of temple servant families continues here. These workers left comfortable homes in Babylon to perform necessary labor for worship in the ruined city. God honors those who gladly do behind-the-scenes work for His people.

These names finish the list of temple servant clans. Many of these families had non-Israelite ancestors, yet they chose to link their lives to God's covenant people. Their loyalty shows that God welcomes all people who dedicate themselves to His service.

These verses list the descendants of Solomon's servants. King Solomon originally organized a group of laborers to help construct the temple and royal buildings, and their families kept that special duty over the centuries. Now they returned to use their skills to rebuild and support the temple community.

The temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants together numbered 392 workers. They are counted as one group because both carried out essential practical duties for the temple. God preserved these helper families so worship could properly restart in Jerusalem.

A group of 642 people returned from towns in Babylon but could not find records to prove they were descended from Israelite families. They were allowed to live with the community, but their tribal roots remained uncertain. God still knows who are His even when human family trees are lost.

Three families claimed to be priests, but their official family scrolls could not be found. One forefather had married into the famous family of Barzillai and taken their name, which blurred his priestly heritage. Because God required proven descent from Aaron to serve at the altar, they were excluded from priestly duties to protect the holiness of worship.

The governor ruled that these men could not eat the most holy food, which was holy sacrificial meat reserved only for priests. They had to wait until a priest could use the Urim and Thummim, sacred lots kept on the high priest's breastpiece to discern God's will. The community chose to pause and wait for God's clear direction rather than guess or disobey His laws.

The total number of Israelites who returned was 42,360 people. They also had 7,337 male and female servants, along with 245 singers to lead music. This large group shows that God preserved a full and active community ready to rebuild their society.

The returning exiles brought many working animals, including horses, mules, camels, and thousands of donkeys. These animals carried luggage, aided travel, and provided muscle for farming. God supplied the practical tools His people needed to begin life again in the land.

The governor led by example and gave generous gifts to the temple treasury. His offering included gold coins called darics, bowls for worship, and 530 garments for the priests. Leaders honor God when they use their own resources to care for His worship and workers.

The family heads and ordinary people also gave large amounts of gold, silver, and priestly robes for the work. Everyone gave according to what they had, following the example of their leaders. When all the people give willingly, God's work has everything it needs to succeed.

The priests, temple workers, and citizens all settled peacefully into their ancestral hometowns. The family lists helped place everyone in their correct property fairly, preventing arguments. By the seventh month of the year, they were settled and prepared to gather for the autumn holy days.
